claims.source: Six additional participants were removed only from source estimation analysis due to technical issues.
claims.evidence: This describes additional data exclusions for specific analyses.

claims.claim: Behavioral results reflecting participants response accuracy on comprehension questions about narratives were significantly above chance (M = 0.715, SD = ± 0.15; t(28)=26.67, p<0.001).
claims.source: Behavioral results reflecting participants response accuracy on comprehension questions about narratives were significantly above chance (M = 0.715, SD = ± 0.15; t(28)=26.67, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This reports the behavioral results with statistical testing.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in behavior as a function of whether task-irrelevant speech was Structured or Non-Structured (t(28)=−0.31, p=0.75).
claims.source: There were no significant differences in behavior as a function of whether task-irrelevant speech was Structured or Non-Structured (t(28)=−0.31, p=0.75; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This reports a null result from behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: Median-split analysis based on neural response to task-irrelevant speech showed no significant differences in performance between participants whose 1 Hz ITPC was above vs. below the median.
claims.source: We performed a between-group t-test on the behavioral results in the Structured condition, and also on the difference between conditions (Structured – Non-Structured). Neither test showed significant differences in performance between participants whose 1 Hz ITPC was above vs. below the median (Structured condition: t(27) = −1.07, p=0.29; Structured – Non-Structured: t(27) = −1.04, p=0.15).
claims.evidence: This reports results from an exploratory analysis examining relationships between neural and behavioral measures.

claims.claim: Scalp-level spectra of the Inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) showed a significant peak at the syllabic-rate (4 Hz) in response to both Structured and Non-Structured hierarchical frequency-tagged speech (p<10^−9; large effect size, Cohen's d > 1.5 in both).
claims.source: Scalp-level spectra of the Inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) showed a significant peak at the syllabic-rate (4 Hz) in response to both Structured and Non-Structured hierarchical frequency-tagged speech, with a four-pole scalp-distribution common to MEG recorded auditory responses (Figure 3a) (p<10^−9; large effect size, Cohen's d > 1.5 in both).
claims.evidence: This reports a key finding from the neural data analysis with statistical results.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between Structured and Non-Structured condition in the 4 Hz response (p=0.899).
claims.source: As expected, there was no significant difference between Structured and Non-Structured condition in the 4 Hz response (p=0.899).
claims.evidence: This reports a null result from the neural data analysis.

claims.claim: A significant peak at 1 Hz was observed in the Structured condition (p<0.003; moderate effect size, Cohen's d = 0.6), but not in the Non-Structured condition (p=0.88).
claims.source: Importantly, we also observed a significant peak at 1 Hz in the Structured condition (p<0.003; moderate effect size, Cohen's d = 0.6), but not in the Non-Structured condition (p=0.88).
claims.evidence: This reports a key finding from the neural data analysis with statistical results.

claims.claim: Comparison of the 1 Hz ITPC between Structured and Non-Structured conditions confirmed a significant difference between them (p=0.045; moderate effect size, Cohen's d = 0.57).
claims.source: Comparison of the 1 Hz ITPC between these conditions also confirmed a significant difference between them (p=0.045; moderate effect size, Cohen's d = 0.57).
claims.evidence: This reports a statistical comparison between conditions.

claims.claim: The scalp-distribution of the 1 Hz peak did not conform to the typical auditory response topography, suggesting different neural generators.
claims.source: The scalp-distribution of the 1 Hz peak did not conform to the typical auditory response topography, suggesting different neural generators.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed scalp topography.

claims.claim: No significant peaks were observed at 2 Hz or 0.5 Hz word and sentence-level rates, nor did the responses at these rates differ significantly between conditions.
claims.source: No other significant peaks were observed at any other frequencies, including the 2 Hz or 0.5 Hz word and sentence-level rates, nor did the responses at these rates differ significantly between conditions.
claims.evidence: This reports null results for other frequencies of interest.

claims.claim: At the source-level, the only significant peaks were at 4 Hz in both conditions (p<10−8; large effect size, Cohen's d > 1.7 in both conditions and both hemispheres) and at 1 Hz in the Structured condition (left hemisphere p=0.052, Cohen's d = 0.43; right hemisphere p<0.007, Cohen's d = 0.6).
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3b, the source-level ITPC spectra, averaged over each hemisphere separately, is qualitatively similar to that observed at the scalp-level. The only significant peaks were at 4 Hz in both conditions (p<10−8; large effect size, Cohen's d > 1.7 in both conditions and both hemispheres) and at 1 Hz in the Structured condition (left hemisphere p=0.052, Cohen's d = 0.43; right hemisphere p<0.007, Cohen's d = 0.6), but not in the Non-Structured condition.
claims.evidence: This reports source-level neural findings with statistical results.

claims.claim: Statistical comparison of the 1 Hz peak between conditions revealed a significant difference between the Structured and Non-Structured condition over the left hemisphere (p=0.026, Cohen's d = 0.57), but not over the right hemisphere (p=0.278).
claims.source: Statistical comparison of the 1 Hz peak between conditions revealed a significant difference between the Structured and Non-Structured condition over the left hemisphere (p=0.026, Cohen's d = 0.57), but not over the right hemisphere (p=0.278).
claims.evidence: This reports a hemispheric difference in the neural response.

claims.claim: The 1 Hz effect in the left hemisphere was observed primarily in frontal and parietal regions, including the inferior-frontal cortex and superior parietal cortex, as well as the mid-cingulate and portions of the middle and superior occipital gyrus (cluster-corrected p=0.002).
claims.source: Figure 3c shows the source-level distribution within the left hemisphere of the difference in 1 Hz ITPC between the Structured and Non-Structured condition. The effect was observed primarily in frontal and parietal regions. Statistical testing evaluating the difference between conditions was performed in 22 pre-determined ROIs per hemisphere, using a permutation test. This indicated significant effects in several ROIs in the left hemisphere including the inferior-frontal cortex and superior parietal cortex, as well as the mid-cingulate and portions of the middle and superior occipital gyrus (cluster-corrected p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This reports the spatial localization of the 1 Hz effect with statistical results.

claims.claim: No ROIs survived multiple-comparison correction in the right hemisphere (cluster-corrected p=0.132), although some ROIs in the right cingulate were significant at an uncorrected level (p<0.05).
claims.source: No ROIs survived multiple-comparison correction in the right hemisphere (cluster-corrected p=0.132), although some ROIs in the right cingulate were significant at an uncorrected level (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This reports null results for the right hemisphere with some uncorrected effects.

claims.claim: The 4 Hz peak was localized to bilateral auditory cortex and did not differ significantly across conditions in either hemisphere (left hemisphere: p=0.155, right hemisphere: p=0.346).
claims.source: With regard to the 4 Hz peak, it was localized as expected to bilateral auditory cortex and did not differ significantly across conditions in either hemisphere (left hemisphere: p=0.155, right hemisphere: p=0.346).
claims.evidence: This reports the localization of the syllable-level response.

claims.claim: No peaks were observed at 2 Hz at the source level and no significant difference between conditions (left hemisphere: p=0.963, right hemisphere: p=0.755).
claims.source: As in the scalp-level data, no peaks were observed at 2 Hz and no significant difference between conditions (left hemisphere: p=0.963, right hemisphere: p=0.755).
claims.evidence: This reports null results for the word-level frequency.

claims.claim: Speech tracking analysis of responses to the to-be-attended narrative yielded robust TRFs (scalp-level predictive power r = 0.1, p<0.01 vs. permutations).
claims.source: Speech tracking analysis of responses to the to-be-attended narrative yielded robust TRFs (scalp-level predictive power r = 0.1, p<0.01 vs. permutations).
claims.evidence: This reports the results of the TRF analysis.

claims.claim: The TRF time-course featured two main peaks, one ~ 80 ms and the other ~140 ms, in line with previous TRF estimations.
claims.source: The TRF time-course featured two main peaks, one ~ 80 ms and the other ~140 ms, in line with previous TRF estimations (Akram et al., 2017; Fiedler et al., 2019; Brodbeck et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This describes the temporal characteristics of the TRF, consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: TRFs were predominantly auditory, localized primarily to auditory cortex (superior temporal gyrus and sulcus; STG/STS) as well as left insula/IFG.
claims.source: Both the scalp-level and source-level TRF analysis indicated that TRFs were predominantly auditory – showing the common four-pole distribution at the scalp-level (Figure 4a) and in the source-level analysis was localized primarily to auditory cortex (superior temporal gyrus and sulcus; STG/STS) as well as left insula/IFG (Figure 4b; 140 ms).
claims.evidence: This reports the spatial localization of the TRF response.

claims.claim: Spatial-temporal clustering permutation test on the scalp-level TRFs revealed significant differences between the conditions between 70–180 ms (p<0.05; cluster corrected).
claims.source: Spatial-temporal clustering permutation test on the scalp-level TRFs revealed significant differences between the conditions between 70–180 ms (p<0.05; cluster corrected), including both the early and late TRF peaks, at a large number of sensors primarily on the left (Figure 4a and c).
claims.evidence: This reports a significant difference in TRFs between conditions.

claims.claim: TRF responses to the to-be-attended speech were enhanced when the task-irrelevant stimulus was Structured vs. Non-Structured.
claims.source: Specifically, TRF responses to the to-be-attended speech were enhanced when the task-irrelevant stimulus was Structured vs. Non-Structured.
claims.evidence: This describes the direction of the effect observed in TRFs.

claims.claim: The TRF enhancement effect was localized at the source-level to a single cluster in the left inferior-frontal cortex, that included portions of the insula and orbito-frontal cortex (spatial-temporal clustering p=0.0058).
claims.source: The effect was observed at the scalp-level with opposite polarity in frontal vs. medial sensors, and was localized at the source-level to a single cluster in the left inferior-frontal cortex, that included portions of the insula and orbito-frontal cortex (Figure 4c; spatial-temporal clustering p=0.0058).
claims.evidence: This reports the spatial localization of the TRF enhancement effect.

claims.claim: Obligatory acoustic representation of task-irrelevant speech was observed, regardless of whether it was Structured or Non-Structured, which manifest as a 4 Hz syllable-level response localized to bilateral auditory regions in the STG/STS.
claims.source: As expected, we observe obligatory acoustic representation of task-irrelevant speech, regardless of whether it was Structured or Non-Structured, which manifest as a 4 Hz syllable-level response localized to bilateral auditory regions in the STG/STS.
claims.evidence: This summarizes a key finding from the study.

claims.claim: For Structured task-irrelevant speech, there is evidence for neural tracking of the phrasal structure, with a 1 Hz peak localized primarily to left inferior-frontal cortex and left posterior-parietal cortex.
claims.source: Critically, for Structured task-irrelevant speech, we also find evidence for neural tracking of the phrasal structure, with a 1 Hz peak localized primarily to left inferior-frontal cortex and left posterior-parietal cortex.
claims.evidence: This summarizes a key finding from the study.

claims.claim: The left inferior-frontal cortex and left posterior-parietal cortex play an important role in speech processing and higher order executive functions.
claims.source: The regions are not associated with low-level processing, but rather play an important role in speech processing and higher order executive functions (Dronkers et al., 2004; Humphries et al., 2006; Linden, 2007; Corbetta et al., 2008; Edin et al., 2009; Hahn et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on brain function.

claims.claim: The speech-tracking response to the to-be-attended speech in left inferior frontal cortex was affected by whether task-irrelevant speech was linguistically Structured or not.
claims.source: Additionally, we find that the speech-tracking response to the to-be-attended speech in left inferior frontal cortex was also affected by whether task-irrelevant speech was linguistically Structured or not.
claims.evidence: This summarizes a key finding from the study.

claims.claim: The results demonstrate that linguistic processes requiring integration of input over relatively long timescales can be applied to task-irrelevant speech.
claims.source: These results contribute to ongoing debates regarding the nature of the competition for processing resources during speech-on-speech masking, demonstrating that linguistic processes requiring integration of input over relatively long timescales can indeed be applied to task-irrelevant speech.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of the broader literature.

claims.claim: Top-down attention is an extremely effective process by which the perceptual and neural representation of task-relevant speech are enhanced at the expense of task-irrelevant stimuli.
claims.source: Top-down attention is an extremely effective process, by which the perceptual and neural representation of task-relevant speech are enhanced at the expense of task-irrelevant stimuli, and speech in particular (Horton et al., 2013; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013b; O'Sullivan et al., 2015; Fiedler et al., 2019; Teoh and Lalor, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: One prominent position is that attention is required for linguistic processing and therefore speech that is outside the focus of attention is not processed beyond its sensory attributes.
claims.source: One prominent position is that attention is required for linguistic processing and therefore speech that is outside the focus of attention is not processed beyond its sensory attributes (Lachter et al., 2004; Brodbeck et al., 2018a; Ding et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical position in the literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The phenomenon of informational masking is often attributed to the detection of familiar acoustic-phonetic features in task-irrelevant speech, that can lead to competition for phonological processing.
claims.source: This effect, referred to as informational masking, is often attributed to the detection of familiar acoustic-phonetic features in task-irrelevant speech, that can lead to competition for phonological processing ('phonological interference') (Durlach et al., 2003; Drullman and Bronkhorst, 2004; Kidd et al., 2008; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008; Rosen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes an interpretation of informational masking, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The phenomenon of informational masking alone is insufficient for determining the extent to which task-irrelevant speech is processed beyond identification of phonological units.
claims.source: However, the phenomenon of informational masking alone is insufficient for determining the extent to which task-irrelevant speech is processed beyond identification of phonological units.
claims.evidence: This is a critical evaluation of the informational masking literature.

claims.claim: An important caveat precludes interpreting ISE findings as clear-cut evidence for semantic processing of task-irrelevant speech: the ISE could be a result of occasional shifts of attention toward task-irrelevant stimuli.
claims.source: However, an important caveat precludes interpreting these findings as clear-cut evidence for semantic processing of task-irrelevant speech: Since these studies primarily involve presentation of arbitrary lists of words (mostly nouns), usually at a relatively slow rate, an alternative explanation is that the ISE is simply a result of occasional shifts of attention toward task-irrelevant stimuli (Carlyon, 2004; Lachter et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This presents an alternative interpretation of ISE findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The effects of informational masking can be attributed to perceptual glimpsing, that is gleaning bits of the task-irrelevant speech in the short 'gaps' in the speech that is to-be-attended.
claims.source: Similarly, the effects of informational masking discussed above can also be attributed to a similar notion of perceptual glimpsing, that is gleaning bits of the task-irrelevant speech in the short 'gaps' in the speech that is to-be-attended (Cooke, 2006; Kidd et al., 2016; Fogerty et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This presents an alternative interpretation of informational masking, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Claims that effects of task-irrelevant speech reflect shifts of attention rather than parallel processing are extremely difficult to reject empirically, as they would require insight into the listeners' internal state of attention.
claims.source: These claims – that effects of task-irrelevant speech are not due to parallel processing but reflect shifts of attention – are extremely difficult to reject empirically, as they would require insight into the listeners' internal state of attention, which at present is not easy to operationalize.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological observation about the challenges in studying attention.

claims.claim: The current study takes a different approach by focusing on linguistic processes that operate over longer timescales rather than detection of single words.
claims.source: In attempt to broach the larger question of processing task-irrelevant speech, the current study takes a different approach by focusing not on detection of single words, but on linguistic processes that operate over longer timescales.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the current study.

claims.claim: The stimuli used in the current study was continuous speech rather than word-lists, whose processing requires accumulating and integrating information over time.
claims.source: To this end the stimuli used here, in both the to-be-attended and the task-irrelevant ear, was continuous speech rather than word-lists whose processing requires accumulating and integrating information over time, which is strikingly different than the point-process nature of listening to word-lists (Fedorenko et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the stimulus design and its rationale, with a citation.

claims.claim: Using continuous speech is more representative of the type of stimuli encountered naturally in the real world.
claims.source: Using continuous speech is also more representative of the type of stimuli encountered naturally in the real world (Hill and Miller, 2010; Risko et al., 2016; Matusz et al., 2019; Shavit-Cohen and Zion Golumbic, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ecological validity.

claims.claim: The phrase-level response observed for task-irrelevant speech is direct indication that phonetic-acoustic information from this stream was decoded and integrated over time, allowing the formation of long-scale representations for phrasal boundaries.
claims.source: Despite the inherent ambiguity regarding the underlying dynamics of attention, the fact that here we observe a phrase-level response for task-irrelevant speech is direct indication that phonetic-acoustic information from this stream was decoded and integrated over time, allowing the formation of long-scale representations for phrasal boundaries.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed phrase-level response.

claims.claim: If the phrase-level response is a result of internal 'glimpsing', this would imply either that the underlying hierarchical speech structure was detected and used to guide 'glimpses' in a rhythmic manner, or that 'glimpses' occur irregularly but sufficient information is gleaned and stored in working-memory.
claims.source: If this is a result of internal 'glimpsing', this would imply either that (a) the underlying hierarchical speech structure was detected and used to guide 'glimpses' in a rhythmic-manner to points in time that are most informative; or (b) that 'glimpses' occur irregularly, but that sufficient information is gleaned through them and stored in working-memory to allow the consistent detection phrasal boundaries in task-irrelevant speech.
claims.evidence: This presents alternative interpretations of the findings based on attention-shifting mechanisms.

claims.claim: Both attention-shifting interpretations imply a sophisticated multiplexed encoding-scheme for successful processing of concurrent speech, that relies on precise temporal control and working-memory storage.
claims.source: Both of these options imply a sophisticated multiplexed encoding-scheme for successful processing of concurrent speech, that relies on precise temporal control and working-memory storage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive mechanisms that would be required under attention-shifting accounts.

claims.claim: Another possibility is that there is no need for attention-shifts and that the system has sufficient capacity to process task-irrelevant speech in parallel to focusing primarily on the to-be-attended stream.
claims.source: Another possibility, of course, is that there is no need for attention-shifts and that the system has sufficient capacity to process task-irrelevant speech in parallel to focusing primarily on the to-be-attended stream.
claims.evidence: This presents an alternative interpretation based on parallel processing.

claims.claim: The current data cannot provide insight into which listening-strategy (attention-shifting vs. parallel processing) underlies the generation of the observed phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech.
claims.source: As mentioned above, the current data cannot provide insight into which of these listening-strategies underlies the generation of the observed phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claims.claim: A recent study by Ding et al., 2018 with similar design did not find significant peaks at any linguistic-related frequencies in the neural response to task-irrelevant speech.
claims.source: The current study is similar in design to another recent study by Ding et al., 2018 where Structured frequency-tagged speech was presented as a task-irrelevant stimulus. In contrast to the results reported here, they did not find significant peaks at any linguistic-related frequencies in the neural response to task-irrelevant speech.
claims.evidence: This compares the current findings to a previous study with different results.

claims.claim: In the study by Ding et al., 2018, to-be-attended speech was time-compressed by a factor of 2.5 and naturally occurring gaps were removed, making the comprehension task substantially more effortful.
claims.source: While in the current experiment to-be-attended speech was presented in its natural form, mimicking the listening effort of real-life speech-processing, in the study by Ding et al., 2018 to-be-attended speech was time-compressed by a factor of 2.5 and naturally occurring gaps were removed, making the comprehension task substantially more effortful (Nourski et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes a key methodological difference between studies, with citations.

claims.claim: Load Theory of Attention proposes that the allocation of processing resources among competing inputs can vary as a function of the perceptual traits and cognitive load imposed by the task.
claims.source: Load Theory of Attention proposes that the allocation of processing resources among competing inputs can vary as a function of the perceptual traits and cognitive load imposed by the task (Lavie et al., 2004; Murphy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical framework, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The divergent results between the current study and Ding et al., 2018 may be due to the extreme difference in the perceptual load and listening effort in the two studies.
claims.source: Accordingly, it is plausible that these divergent results are due to the extreme difference in the perceptual load and listening effort in the two studies.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differences between studies.

claims.claim: If understanding the to-be-attended speech imposes relatively low perceptual and cognitive load, then sufficient resources may be available to additionally process aspects of task-irrelevant speech.
claims.source: Specifically, if understanding the to-be-attended speech imposes relatively low perceptual and cognitive load, then sufficient resources may be available to additionally process aspects of task-irrelevant speech, but that this might not be the case as the task becomes more difficult and perceptually demanding (Wild et al., 2012; Gagné et al., 2017; Peelle, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on load theory, with citations.

claims.claim: The current results provide a non-trivial positive example for processing task-irrelevant speech that is processed beyond its acoustic attributes, in an experimental context that closely emulates the perceptual and cognitive load encountered in real-life.
claims.source: The current results provide a non-trivial positive example for processing task-irrelevant speech that is indeed processed beyond its acoustic attributes, in an experimental context that closely emulates the perceptual and cognitive load encountered in real-life (despite the admitted unnatural nature of the task-irrelevant speech).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's contribution to the literature.

claims.claim: The results invite adopting a more flexible perspective of processing bottlenecks within the speech processing system, that takes into consideration the perceptual and cognitive load imposed in a given context.
claims.source: Rather, they invite adopting a more flexible perspective of processing bottlenecks within the speech processing system, that takes into consideration the perceptual and cognitive load imposed in a given context, in line with load theory of attention (Mattys et al., 2012; Lavie et al., 2014; Fairnie et al., 2016; Gagné et al., 2017; Peelle, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Others have observed that the level of processing applied to task-irrelevant stimuli can be affected by task demands.
claims.source: Supporting this perspective, others have also observed that the level of processing applied to task-irrelevant stimuli can be affected by task demands (Hohlfeld and Sommer, 2005; Pulvermüller et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Individual differences in attentional abilities, and particularly the ability to process concurrent speech, have been attributed partially to working-memory capacity.
claims.source: Moreover, individual differences in attentional abilities, and particularly the ability to process concurrent speech, have been attributed partially to working-memory capacity, a trait associated with the availability of more cognitive resources (Beaman et al., 2007; Forster and Lavie, 2008; Naveh-Benjamin et al., 2014; Lambez et al., 2020) but cf. (Elliott and Briganti, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research, with a contrasting citation.

claims.claim: The fronto-temporal cluster, which included the IFG and insula, is known to play an important role in speech processing.
claims.source: The fronto-temporal cluster, which included the IFG and insula, is known to play an important role in speech processing (Dronkers et al., 2004; Humphries et al., 2006; Brodbeck et al., 2018b; Blank and Fedorenko, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on brain function.

claims.claim: The left IFG and insula are particularly associated with linguistic processes that require integration over longer periods of time, such as syntactic structure building and semantic integration of meaning.
claims.source: The left IFG and insula are particularly associated with linguistic processes that require integration over longer periods of time, such as syntactic structure building and semantic integration of meaning (Fedorenko et al., 2016; Matchin et al., 2017; Schell et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on brain function.

claims.claim: The left IFG and insula are recruited when speech comprehension requires effort, such as for degraded or noise-vocoded speech.
claims.source: and are also recruited when speech comprehension requires effort, such as for degraded or noise-vocoded speech (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003; Obleser and Kotz, 2010; Davis et al., 2011; Hervais-Adelman et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on brain function.

claims.claim: Observing a phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech in left IFG and insula is in line with their functional involvement in processing speech under adverse conditions.
claims.source: Accordingly, observing a phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech in these regions is in line with their functional involvement in processing speech under adverse conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in light of known brain function.

claims.claim: Both the posterior-parietal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus play an important role in verbal working-memory.
claims.source: However, both the posterior-parietal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus play an important role in verbal working-memory (Todd and Marois, 2004; Postle et al., 2006; Linden, 2007; McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Edin et al., 2009; Østby et al., 2011; Rottschy et al., 2012; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012; Ma et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2015; Yue et al., 2019; Fedorenko and Blank, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous research on brain function.

claims.claim: Detecting the phrasal structure of task-irrelevant speech, while focusing primarily on processing the to-be-attended narratives, likely requires substantial working-memory for integrating chunks of information over time.
claims.source: Detecting the phrasal structure of task-irrelevant speech, while focusing primarily on processing the to-be-attended narratives, likely requires substantial working-memory for integrating chunks of information over time.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive demands of the task.

claims.claim: Attention and working-memory are tightly linked constructs.
claims.source: Indeed, attention and working-memory are tightly linked constructs (McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012; Vandierendonck, 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The ability to control and maintain attention is often associated with individual working-memory capacity.
claims.source: and as mentioned above, the ability to control and maintain attention is often associated with individual working-memory capacity (Cowan et al., 2005; Beaman et al., 2007; Forster and Lavie, 2008; Naveh-Benjamin et al., 2014; Lambez et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: One possible interpretation for the presence of a phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech in the left posterior-parietal cortex and inferior frontal regions is their role in forming and maintaining a representation of task-irrelevant stimuli in working-memory.
claims.source: Therefore, one possible interpretation for the presence of a phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech in the left posterior-parietal cortex and inferior frontal regions, is their role in forming and maintaining a representation of task-irrelevant stimuli in working-memory, perhaps as a means for monitoring the environment for potentially important events.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: In previous studies using the same stimuli in a single-speaker context, a prominent peak was observed at both the word- and the phrase-rate.
claims.source: Regarding the lack of a word-level response at 2 Hz for Structured task-irrelevant stimuli, this was indeed surprising, since in previous studies using the same stimuli in a single-speaker context we observe a prominent peak at both the word- and the phrase-rate (Makov et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This compares the current findings to previous research using the same stimuli.

claims.claim: One possibility for the lack of a 2 Hz peak is that the task-irrelevant speech was indeed parsed into words, but that the neural signature of 2 Hz parsing was not observable due to interference from the acoustic contributions at 2 Hz.
claims.source: One possibility is that the task-irrelevant speech was indeed parsed into words as well, but that the neural signature of 2 Hz parsing was not observable due to interference from the acoustic contributions at 2 Hz (see Supplementary Materials and Luo and Ding, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the null result, with a citation.

claims.claim: Another possibility is that the lack of a word-level response for task-irrelevant speech indicates that it does not undergo full lexical analysis.
claims.source: However, another possibility is that the lack of a word-level response for task-irrelevant speech indicates that it does not undergo full lexical analysis.
claims.evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the null result.

claims.claim: There is substantial evidence that lexical and syntactic processes are separable and dissociable cognitive processes, that rely on partially different neural substrates.
claims.source: Counter to the linear intuition that syntactic structuring depends on identifying individual lexemes, there is substantial evidence that lexical and syntactic processes are separable and dissociable cognitive processes, that rely on partially different neural substrates (Friederici and Kotz, 2003; Hagoort, 2003; Humphries et al., 2006; Nelson et al., 2017; Schell et al., 2017; Pylkkänen, 2019; Morgan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's contribution, based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: The findings that the speech tracking response of the to-be-attended narratives is enhanced when competing with a Structured task-irrelevant speech, specifically left inferior-frontal brain regions, pinpoints the locus of this competition to these dedicated speech-processing regions.
claims.source: The findings that the speech tracking response of the to-be-attended narratives is enhanced when competing with a Structured task-irrelevant speech, specifically left inferior-frontal brain regions, where we also observed tracking of the phrase-structure of task-irrelevant speech, pinpoints the locus of this competition to these dedicated speech-processing regions, above and beyond any sensory-level competition (Davis et al., 2011; Brouwer et al., 2012; Hervais-Adelman et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, with citations.

claims.claim: The enhanced speech tracking response in IFG reflects the investment of additional listening effort for comprehending the task-relevant speech.

claims.claim: The lack of a behavioral effect is attributed primarily to the insensitivity of the behavioral measures used, which consisted of asking four multiple-choice questions after each 45 s long narrative.
claims.source: Since the neural response to the to-be-attended speech was modulated by the type of competition it faced, then why was this not mirrored in the current behavioral results as well? In the current study participants achieved similar accuracy rates on the comprehension questions regardless of whether the natural-narratives were paired with Structured or Non-Structured stimuli in the task-irrelevant ear, and there was no significant correlation between the neural effects and performance. We attribute the lack of a behavioral effect primarily to the insensitivity of the behavioral measures used here, that consisted of asking four multiple-choice questions after each 45 s long narrative.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the null behavioral result.

claims.claim: Numerous previous studies have been able to demonstrate behavioral 'intrusions' of the task-irrelevant stimuli on performance of an attended-task using more constrained experimental paradigms.
claims.source: Although numerous previous studies have been able to demonstrate behavioral 'intrusions' of the task-irrelevant stimuli on performance of an attended-task, these have been shown using more constrained experimental paradigms, that have the advantage of probing behavior at a finer scale, but are substantially less ecological (e.g. memory-recall for short lists of words or priming effects; Tun et al., 2002; Dupoux et al., 2003; Rivenez et al., 2006; Rivenez et al., 2008; Carey et al., 2014; Aydelott et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In moving toward studying speech processing and attention under more ecological circumstances, there is an experimental challenge of obtaining sufficiently sensitive behavior measures without disrupting listening.
claims.source: In moving toward studying speech processing and attention under more ecological circumstances, using natural continuous speech, we face an experimental challenge of obtaining sufficiently sensitive behavior measures without disrupting listening with an ongoing task (e.g. target detection) or encroaching too much on working-memory.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological observation about challenges in ecological research.

claims.claim: The challenge of obtaining sensitive behavioral measures is shared by many previous studies and is one of the main motivations for turning directly to the brain and studying neural activity during uninterrupted listening to continuous speech.
claims.source: This is a challenge shared by many previous studies similar to ours, and is one of the main motivations for turning directly to the brain and studying neural activity during uninterrupted listening to continuous speech, rather than relying on sparse behavioral indications (Ding et al., 2016; Makov et al., 2017; Brodbeck et al., 2018a; Broderick et al., 2018; Broderick et al., 2019; Donhauser and Baillet, 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological approach in the field, with citations.

claims.claim: The results indicate that even though top-down attention effectively enables listeners to focus on a particular task-relevant source of input, this prioritization can be affected by the nature of task-irrelevant sounds.
claims.source: The current study contributes to ongoing efforts to understand how the brain deals with the abundance of auditory inputs in our environment. Our results indicate that even though top-down attention effectively enables listeners to focus on a particular task-relevant source of input (speech in this case), this prioritization can be affected by the nature of task-irrelevant sounds.
claims.evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.claim: When task-irrelevant input constitutes meaningful speech, left fronto-temporal speech-processing regions are engaged in processing both stimuli, potentially leading to competition for resources and more effortful listening.
claims.source: Specifically, we find that when the latter constitutes meaningful speech, left fronto-temporal speech-processing regions are engaged in processing both stimuli, potentially leading to competition for resources and more effortful listening.
claims.evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.source: Additional brain regions, such as the PPC, are also engaged in representing some aspects of the linguistic structure of task-irrelevant speech, which we interpret as maintaining a representation of what goes on in the 'rest of the environment', in case something important arises.

claims.claim: Similar interactions between the structure of task-irrelevant sounds and responses to the to-be-attended sounds have been previously demonstrated for non-verbal stimuli as well.
claims.source: Importantly, similar interactions between the structure of task-irrelevant sounds and responses to the to-be-attended sounds have been previously demonstrated for non-verbal stimuli as well (Makov and Zion Golumbic, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Attentional selection is not an all-or-none processes, but rather is a dynamic process of balancing the resources allocated to competing input, which is highly affected by the specific perceptual, cognitive and environmental aspects of a given task.
claims.source: Together, this highlights the fact that attentional selection is not an all-or-none processes, but rather is a dynamic process of balancing the resources allocated to competing input, which is highly affected by the specific perceptual, cognitive and environmental aspects of a given task.
claims.evidence: This is a broad theoretical conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

results.result: The study employed a dichotic listening paradigm with MEG recording in 30 native Hebrew speakers. Participants attended to natural speech narratives in one ear while task-irrelevant stimuli (either linguistically Structured or Non-Structured isochronous syllables at 4 Hz) were presented to the other ear. The experimental design included careful acoustic control, frequency-tagging of linguistic hierarchies, and appropriate participant familiarization procedures.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C55 collectively describe a well-designed experimental paradigm with appropriate controls, validated stimuli, proper sample size justification (C29), and ethical approval (C30). The acoustic properties of stimuli were carefully characterized (C40-C44), and methodological procedures including familiarization (C49-C50) and data acquisition parameters (C51-C52) are clearly documented. The experimental design appropriately addresses the research question.

results.result: Behavioral performance on comprehension questions about attended narratives was significantly above chance (M=0.715, p<0.001), but showed no significant differences between Structured and Non-Structured conditions. Median-split analysis based on neural responses also revealed no relationship between behavioral performance and neural tracking of task-irrelevant speech.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 report behavioral results with appropriate statistical tests. The finding that performance was above chance validates that participants attended to the target speech. The null results for condition differences (C57, C58) are properly reported with statistics. However, as the authors acknowledge (C133), the behavioral measure may lack sensitivity to detect subtle effects.

results.result: At the scalp level, both Structured and Non-Structured task-irrelevant speech elicited significant 4 Hz (syllable-rate) responses with no difference between conditions. Critically, only Structured speech elicited a significant 1 Hz (phrase-rate) response (p<0.003, Cohen's d=0.6), which differed significantly from Non-Structured speech (p=0.045, Cohen's d=0.57). No significant peaks were observed at 2 Hz or 0.5 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 report the primary neural findings with appropriate statistics, effect sizes, and comparisons. The 4 Hz response validates acoustic processing of task-irrelevant speech (C59-C60), while the selective 1 Hz response to Structured speech (C61-C62) provides direct evidence for phrasal structure tracking. The scalp topography difference (C63) suggests distinct neural generators. Statistical tests are appropriate and properly reported.

results.result: Source-level analysis localized the 1 Hz phrase-rate response to Structured task-irrelevant speech primarily to left inferior-frontal cortex and superior parietal cortex (cluster-corrected p=0.002), with significant hemispheric lateralization (left: p=0.026; right: p=0.278). The 4 Hz syllable-rate response localized to bilateral auditory cortex without condition differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 provide source localization with appropriate statistical corrections for multiple comparisons. The left-lateralized fronto-parietal localization of the phrase-level response (C67) is consistent with known language processing networks. The bilateral auditory localization of syllable-level responses (C69) is expected. The use of 22 pre-defined ROIs and cluster correction (C67) provides appropriate control for multiple comparisons.

results.result: TRF analysis of neural tracking of to-be-attended speech revealed robust responses (r=0.1, p<0.01) localized to auditory cortex and left inferior-frontal regions. Critically, TRF responses in left inferior-frontal cortex were significantly enhanced (70-180 ms, p<0.05 cluster-corrected) when competing with Structured versus Non-Structured task-irrelevant speech (source-level: p=0.0058).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 report TRF findings with appropriate validation against permutations (C71), consistency with prior literature (C72), and proper spatial-temporal clustering statistics (C74, C76). The enhancement of attended speech tracking in IFG when competing with Structured speech (C75-C76) provides evidence for competition at the linguistic processing level. Statistical methods are appropriate and properly applied.

results.result: The study demonstrates that phrasal structure of task-irrelevant speech is represented in neural responses in left inferior-frontal and posterior-parietal regions, indicating that selective attention does not fully eliminate linguistic processing of task-irrelevant speech. This provides evidence that linguistic processes requiring integration over relatively long timescales can be applied to task-irrelevant speech.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C78, C81, and C92 represent the core interpretation of the 1 Hz neural response findings. The presence of phrase-level tracking (C2, C78) in higher-order language regions provides strong evidence that task-irrelevant speech undergoes linguistic processing beyond acoustic features (C3, C81). The interpretation that this reflects temporal integration (C92) is well-supported by the experimental design using hierarchical frequency-tagging.

results.result: Neural tracking of to-be-attended speech in left inferior-frontal cortex was enhanced when competing with Structured versus Non-Structured task-irrelevant speech, suggesting inherent competition between attended and task-irrelevant speech for linguistic processing resources. This enhancement reflects increased listening effort and pinpoints the locus of competition to dedicated speech-processing regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C80, C123, C124, C131, and C132 interpret the TRF enhancement findings. The enhanced neural response to attended speech when competing with Structured speech (C4, C123) is well-documented in the data. The interpretation as reflecting competition for linguistic resources (C5, C124, C131) is reasonable given the localization to IFG and the experimental control for acoustic factors. The listening effort interpretation (C132) is plausible though somewhat speculative.

results.result: The study acknowledges that the observed phrase-level response to task-irrelevant speech could result from either attention-shifting mechanisms (requiring sophisticated temporal control and working memory) or parallel processing capacity. The current data cannot distinguish between these alternative mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 appropriately acknowledge a fundamental limitation of the study. The authors correctly note that both attention-shifting and parallel processing could explain the phrase-level response (C93, C95), and honestly state that the data cannot distinguish between these mechanisms (C96). This represents appropriate scientific caution and identifies an important direction for future research.

results.result: The study's findings differ from Ding et al. (2018), which found no linguistic processing of task-irrelevant speech. This discrepancy may be explained by differences in perceptual load: the current study used natural speech while Ding et al. used time-compressed speech. This suggests that processing of task-irrelevant speech may depend on the cognitive load imposed by the attended task, consistent with Load Theory of Attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C103 present a speculative but plausible interpretation of divergent findings. The methodological difference is accurately described (C98), and the Load Theory framework (C99) provides a reasonable explanatory mechanism (C100-C101). However, this remains speculative (C100 explicitly states this is 'plausible') and would require systematic manipulation of perceptual load to test directly. The interpretation is reasonable but not definitively supported.

results.result: The left inferior-frontal cortex and insula, where phrase-level responses were observed, are known to play important roles in speech processing, particularly for linguistic processes requiring temporal integration such as syntactic structure building, and are recruited during effortful speech comprehension. The observed phrase-level response in these regions is consistent with their functional role in processing speech under adverse conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 and C79 interpret the functional significance of the observed brain regions based on extensive prior literature (well-cited in C106-C108). The interpretation that IFG/insula involvement reflects linguistic processing under adverse conditions (C109) is well-supported by the citations and consistent with the experimental findings. This represents appropriate integration of current findings with established neuroscience literature.

results.result: The posterior-parietal cortex and inferior-frontal regions, which showed phrase-level responses, play important roles in verbal working memory. The phrase-level response in these regions may reflect their role in forming and maintaining a representation of task-irrelevant speech in working memory, possibly for monitoring the environment for important events.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 present a speculative interpretation of the parietal findings. While the role of these regions in working memory is well-established (C110, extensively cited), the specific interpretation that they maintain representations of task-irrelevant speech for environmental monitoring (C114) is explicitly speculative ('one possible interpretation'). This is a reasonable hypothesis but lacks direct supporting evidence from the current study.

results.result: No word-level (2 Hz) response was observed for task-irrelevant speech, despite previous studies showing such responses when the same stimuli were attended. This could reflect either acoustic interference at 2 Hz or indicate that task-irrelevant speech does not undergo full lexical analysis. Evidence suggests lexical and syntactic processes are dissociable, and phrasal structure can be detected without full lexical processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C70, and C115-C120 address the absence of word-level responses. The null finding is properly reported (C64, C70), and the comparison to previous studies (C115) is appropriate. However, the interpretation remains uncertain: the authors present two competing explanations (acoustic interference C116 vs. incomplete lexical processing C117, C120) and cannot distinguish between them. The supporting evidence for dissociable lexical/syntactic processing (C118-C119) is well-cited but doesn't resolve the ambiguity in the current data.

results.result: The lack of behavioral differences between conditions is attributed to insensitivity of the behavioral measure (four multiple-choice questions per 45-second narrative). Previous studies showing behavioral effects used more constrained paradigms. Studying speech processing under ecological conditions presents challenges in obtaining sensitive behavioral measures without disrupting natural listening.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 provide a reasonable explanation for the null behavioral findings. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation of their behavioral measure (C133) and contextualize this within the broader challenge of ecological research (C135-C136). The comparison to previous studies (C134) is well-cited. This represents honest acknowledgment of methodological limitations and trade-offs in ecological validity.

results.result: The study demonstrates that attentional selection is not an all-or-none process but rather a dynamic process of balancing resources allocated to competing inputs. When task-irrelevant input constitutes meaningful speech, left fronto-temporal regions process both stimuli, leading to competition for resources. Additional regions like posterior-parietal cortex represent aspects of task-irrelevant speech structure, possibly for environmental monitoring.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 and C141 present the study's main conclusions, which are well-supported by the empirical findings. The evidence for processing of both attended and task-irrelevant speech in overlapping brain regions (C138) is directly demonstrated by the neural data. The interpretation of attentional selection as a dynamic, context-dependent process (C141) is supported by the findings and consistent with Load Theory. The environmental monitoring interpretation (C139) is more speculative but reasonable.

results.result: The introduction establishes the theoretical context and debate regarding linguistic processing of task-irrelevant speech. Historical research shows attention enhances attended speech at the expense of task-irrelevant input, but the extent of linguistic processing of task-irrelevant speech remains debated. Evidence exists for both Early-Selection (attention required for linguistic processing) and Late-Selection (parallel processing) theories. The current study addresses this by focusing on linguistic processes operating over longer timescales using continuous speech.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C18 and C82-C91 provide appropriate background and context, all well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The authors accurately characterize the state of the field, including conflicting findings and theoretical debates. The rationale for the current study's approach (C89-C91) follows logically from the identified gaps in previous research. This represents thorough and accurate literature review.

results.result: Hierarchical frequency-tagging methodology allows probing whether linguistic processes requiring integration over longer timescales are applied to task-irrelevant speech. If neural signals show peaks at frequencies associated with linguistic features of Structured speech, this would provide evidence for integration-based processes operating on longer timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C19 and C26 describe the methodological rationale, which is well-supported by citations to previous work establishing this technique (C19). The logical inference about what frequency peaks would indicate (C26) is sound and follows from the frequency-tagging design. This represents appropriate application of an established methodology to a novel question.

results.result: The speech-tracking response to attended speech was localized to auditory and left inferior-frontal regions, consistent with previous studies. The response in auditory regions was similar across conditions, but left inferior-frontal cortex showed modulation by task-irrelevant speech type. This demonstrates that interference occurs at higher linguistic levels beyond phonetic-acoustic competition, as all low-level features were perfectly controlled between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C130 interpret the TRF findings in the context of prior literature and the experimental design. The localization is consistent with previous work (C121, well-cited). The interpretation that enhanced IFG responses reflect linguistic-level competition (C130-C131) is well-supported by the experimental control for acoustic factors (C24-C25, C130). The comparison to previous studies (C127-C128) is appropriately cited.
